candidates.title: Prohibition on the sale or use of coordinated pricing algorithms to set rents or manage occupancy levels (BMC Chapter 13.63)
candidates.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to Berkeley landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley. It is also unlawful for a landlord to use such an algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels. A coordinated pricing algorithm is a computation process that uses non-public Competitor Data (less than 90 days old) to recommend rents, fees, occupancy rates or other lease terms in coordination between a Berkeley landlord and its competitors, including through a third-party vendor. The chapter does not cap rents. Each month a violation continues and each unit for which the algorithm was used is a separate violation. The City Attorney may sue for damages, injunctive relief, restitution and civil penalties. An aggrieved tenant may sue the landlord for injunctive relief, damages and civil penalties, with prevailing-party attorney's fees.

candidates.coverage_conditions: All residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley; applies to landlords and to sellers or licensors of such algorithms to Berkeley landlords.
candidates.exemptions: Excluded from the definition of coordinated pricing algorithm: (a) products or processes that publish aggregated, anonymous rental data without recommending rents, fees, occupancy rates or terms; (b) products used to set rent or income limits under affordable housing guidelines of a local, state or federal government; (c) products or processes used for market research for project financing, appraisals, or research, testing or training for software development, provided Competitor Data is not an input when a recommendation is calculated for a Berkeley landlord.

candidates.title: California Tenant Protection Act: just cause required to terminate tenancies
candidates.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months (or 24 months if an additional adult tenant was added before an existing tenant reached 24 months), the owner may not terminate the tenancy without just cause stated in the written termination notice. At-fault just causes include nonpayment of rent, breach of a material lease term, nuisance, waste, refusal to sign a lease extension, criminal activity, unauthorized subletting, refusal of lawful entry, unlawful use, and failure to vacate after termination or after giving notice. No-fault just causes include owner or family move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, compliance with a government or court order or local ordinance, and demolition or substantial remodel. Curable violations require a notice to cure before a three-day notice to quit. For no-fault terminations the owner must give relocation assistance equal to one month's rent within 15 calendar days of service of the notice, or waive the final month's rent. The notice must state the tenant's right to this. Owner move-in requires occupancy within 90 days for at least 12 months, and tenants get re-rental rights if the demolition or remodel is not carried out. Owners must give tenants a notice about these protections. Waivers are void.

candidates.title: Massachusetts security deposit limits, handling, interest and return (M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B)
candidates.requirement: A security deposit may not exceed the first month's rent. It must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, and the tenant must get a receipt within 30 days naming the bank, location, amount and account number. The tenant must get a signed receipt when the deposit is received, and a written statement of the premises' condition within 10 days after tenancy commences or on receipt of the deposit, whichever is later. If the lessor holds the deposit for a year or longer, it must pay interest at 5% per year (or the lesser amount actually received from the bank) at the end of each year of the tenancy. The lessor must return the deposit, less permitted deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. Permitted deductions are unpaid rent or water charges, unpaid tax increases under a conforming escalation clause, and reasonable repair of damage beyond normal wear and tear. Damage deductions require a sworn itemized list with cost evidence within the same 30 days. The lessor must keep deposit records for 2 years after the tenancy ends. The deposit and accrued interest must be transferred to a successor in interest. As amended effective Aug 1, 2025, the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities may by regulation authorize an optional fee in lieu of a security deposit, capped at 1 month's rent in total with any deposit.

candidates.title: New Jersey Fair Chance in Housing Act (criminal record screening limits)
candidates.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about an applicant's criminal record, orally or in writing, or require an application that includes such inquiries, before making a conditional offer. The only exceptions are methamphetamine manufacture on the premises of federally assisted housing, and lifetime sex offender registration. Before or after a conditional offer, providers may not evaluate applicants on arrests or charges without conviction, expunged convictions, pardoned convictions, vacated or nullified convictions, juvenile adjudications, or sealed records. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions may be considered: murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, sexual assault, certain child sexual-act offenses, or any crime resulting in lifetime sex offender registration; first-degree indictable offenses within 6 years; second- or third-degree offenses within 4 years; fourth-degree offenses within 1 year (measured from the conviction or the end of any prison sentence). A conditional offer may be withdrawn only if the provider determines by a preponderance of the evidence that withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, after an individualized assessment of six factors. The provider must give written notice stating the specific reasons and an opportunity to appeal with evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. Applicants may request the information relied on within 30 days of the withdrawal notice, and the provider must supply it free of charge within 10 days. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is part of its eligibility criteria and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracy or rehabilitation. Housing advertisements may not state that applicants with arrests or convictions will not be considered. Providers may not require drug or alcohol tests or consent to obtain drug treatment facility information. Criminal records may not be disseminated or used for purposes inconsistent with the act. Enforcement is by complaint to the Division on Civil Rights, with no court action by private parties.

(p) Civil-court liability for theft, assault or threats, or drug activity. (q) Theft from the landlord or from tenants in the same building. (r) Human trafficking. Under (n), (o) and (p), no suit may be brought more than two years after the juvenile adjudication, the conviction or the release from incarceration, whichever is later. Under (r), no suit may be brought more than two years after the violation ended. Under (n)-(q), a Notice to Quit must be served at least 3 days before suit. Notice to quit: 3 months for at-will or year-to-year tenancies, 1 month for month-to-month tenancies, and 3 days for the disorderly, destructive or rule/lease-violation causes. Before evicting after a foreclosure sale to an owner-occupant buyer, a 90-day notice to quit is required, and a lease running past 90 days must expire first. candidates.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
candidates.requirement: Makes it unlawful, and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, for a rental property owner (or its agent, representative or subcontractor) to pay for or subscribe to the services of a coordinator. It is also unlawful for a coordinator to facilitate a tacit or express agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition, including by performing a coordinating function. Two or more persons may not engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination. Agents or representatives of a coordinator may not engage in parallel pricing coordination. No person may perform a coordinating function. A coordinating function includes collecting competitively sensitive information of two or more owners to train or run an algorithm that sets or recommends rents, lease terms or occupancy levels. It also includes setting rents, lease terms or occupancy levels with an algorithm that uses other owners' competitively sensitive information. Finally, it includes recommending the same or a substantially similar algorithmic output to two or more owners in a way that facilitates parallel pricing coordination. Exclusions: research, statistical analysis or testing not used to set or recommend terms; free public rent estimates; real estate brokerage databases available on equal terms that do not set or recommend prices; and government entities setting rents through affordability controls. The Attorney General must set up a complaint location and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.

candidates.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protections (Just Cause for Termination of Tenancy)
candidates.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a tenancy without just cause. At-fault causes include non-payment of rent, material lease breach, nuisance, waste, refusal to sign a substantially similar lease renewal, criminal activity or criminal threat, unlawful sublet, refusal of lawful entry, unlawful use, failure to vacate after employment ends, and failure to deliver possession after the tenant's own notice. No-fault causes, which must be in good faith, are owner or family move-in (minimum 12 continuous months, with the occupant moving in within 90 days), withdrawal from the rental market, compliance with a government or court vacate order or local ordinance, and demolition or substantial remodel. Termination notices must state the cause. No-fault notices must be given 30 or 60 days ahead under Civ.
